notes.heading: Interpret a bit pattern using an explicit encoding
paragraphs: A bit pattern has no unique meaning without its encoding. The same eight bits can represent an unsigned number, a signed number, part of a character or a colour component. In an eight-bit two's-complement integer, the most significant bit has weight -128 and the remaining weights are positive powers of two. Fixed width also limits which arithmetic results fit. Character count and byte count differ for variable-length encodings, so storage calculations need the actual encoding and assumptions about overhead rather than a universal one-byte-per-character rule.

questions.prompt: Interpret 11111101 as both an 8-bit unsigned integer and an 8-bit two's-complement integer.
solution: For two's complement, replace the leading 128 weight with -128, equivalently subtract 256.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit unsigned counter uses wraparound arithmetic. It contains 250 and is increased by 12. Give the mathematical sum and the stored value.
questions.answer: The mathematical sum is 262; the stored value is 6.
solution: Reduce 262 modulo 256 under the stated wraparound rule.

questions.prompt: A fictional message contains 40 ASCII characters encoded in UTF-8 plus 10 other characters, each specified to take 3 bytes. Ignoring overhead, calculate bytes and explain why counting 50 characters is insufficient.
questions.answer: 70 bytes; variable byte lengths mean 50 characters need not mean 50 bytes.
solution: Add 10×3=30 bytes, using the stated encoding lengths.
markingPoints: Explain character count versus byte count.
